meta.sourceSheet: worksheet 'map-cards' of the designer spreadsheet (crate columns), plus the rulebook for the seat-scaling tables. The VP and money columns of that sheet are SUPERSEDED by the flat island - see the note below.
notes: THE FLAT ISLAND (owner, 2026-08-09). The island lost its hierarchy in one decision. Every tile in play is now mechanically identical: 2 crates of 2 cards, £1 on delivery, 6 VP to the first deliverer and 3 VP to the second. There is no level gate, no ascending 4/8/16 size gradient, no per-level fill-order bonus, and no level-3 end trigger. The game ends when any one seat completes its 6th island delivery. Everything that used to be decided by a tile's LEVEL is now decided by its DELIVERY ORDER, which is the single gradient left in the island and the only thing worth racing for.

LEVEL IS NOW ART. `tiles[].level` and `slotsBySeats` survive because the physical island is still built as a pyramid out of the printed map cards, and the bookend rule below still decides which faces are on the table. Nothing mechanical reads a level. If you find yourself adding a rule keyed to level, you are re-introducing the hierarchy that was just deleted - price it as a new rule, not as a restoration.

vpByDeliveryOrder is the whole VP schedule and the whole capacity rule at once: entry i is the VP taken by the (i+1)th delivery to a tile, and the array's LENGTH is how many deliveries a tile accepts. There is deliberately no separate deliveriesPerTile knob. Lengthening the array is the only way to open a third delivery space, which forces the question 'and what is it worth?' to be answered in the same edit. 6 then 3 is the time gradient in its entirety: being first to a tile is worth double being second, it is printed on the tile rather than on a chit strip beside the board, and it needs no per-player-count row in the teach. It replaces fillOrderBonusBySeats, which is deleted - see Rulebook/outstanding-rule-changes.md change 4 for why two overlapping decaying rewards was one too many.

tileRule replaces levelRules. crates x cardsPerCrate = 4 barn cards, at every tile, at every seat count. The 2/4/6 chain by level is gone, as is the 2/3/4 coin chain: coinsPerDelivery is a flat £1. HISTORY, so nobody re-derives the old numbers off the sheet: ticket 14 read the printed quantity label as 2=/3=/3= and settled 2/6/9 on 2026-08-02; ticket 38 overturned it the same day to 2/4/6; the flat island overturned both on 2026-08-09. PRINT CONSEQUENCE: every tile face must now show TWO crates and the label 2=, so the map-cards worksheet needs its crate count and quantity label reworked at levels 1 and 3 (level 2 already prints two crates, and its 3= label was already wrong).

cardsPerSubstitution is the WILD SUBSTITUTION (owner, 2026-08-08, kept through the flat island): when you pay the island, any single card it asks for may instead be paid with this many cards of any crops. null switches the rule off and restores exact matching, which is the control arm. It is the answer to ticket 38's finding that the barn queue is a MATCHING problem and not a quantity one - 88.8% of barn-holding decisions cannot afford any open tile and 84% of those are 1-2 cards short. Because a crate is 2 cards of ONE named suit, all or nothing, a single odd card of a suit is worth exactly zero and a barn fills with cards that can never combine: a parity trap. A substitution rate of 2 breaks the trap at a real price. The property that makes 2 the right number rather than a tuned one: the valve OPENS AS THE PRESSURE RISES. A 4-card barn can afford one substitution, a 12-card barn can afford six, so the rule cannot cheapen delivery in the early game when barns are small and always rescues a jammed late game. SCOPE IS LOAD-BEARING: island delivery ONLY. It must never reach the balloon move cost, a build cost, or anything else that spends barn cards, or the barn stops being a dead end and starts accelerating engines. NOTE the flat island changed its ceiling: the dearest all-wild payment used to be a 12-card Level 3 tile and is now 8 cards at any tile, so the rule is flatter and more often affordable than the 2026-08-08 measurement saw it.

The END TRIGGER lives in rules.json (endGame.trigger = deliveryCount, deliveriesToTrigger = 6) rather than here, because it is no longer a property of any tile. It is FLAT at every seat count, which is a deliberate asymmetry the owner took with the trade named: 6 deliveries is half of the 2-seat island's 12 delivery spaces, a third of the 3-seat island's 18 and a quarter of the 4-seat island's 24, so relative to the board the 2-player game runs longest. Watch it at 2p before dialling anything.
Coins are not seeded onto a tile. The bank pays tileRule.coinsPerDelivery on EVERY delivery, first and second alike.

Delivery cost is PER CRATE. A tile prints one crate icon per demand, a quantity label beside it, and one suit token slot per crate. The quantity label is the RATE, not the total - it reads 2=, meaning 2 cards of ONE suit per crate. A suit demand token is placed face up on every crate at setup, and paying a crate costs cardsPerCrate barn cards of that crate's suit. A cornucopia token is wild and accepts any suit at the same rate. Two crates on one tile may be dealt the same suit, in which case the tile wants 4 cards of one crop; that is the pool doing its job, not a bug.
seats counts players at the table. There is no one-seat board: a solo game is a two-seat game in which a bot occupies the second seat.

Exactly (seats + 1) suit decks are in play: one owned by each seat, plus one passive suit nobody farms but everybody may draw from and the island demands. The remaining suits are out of the game entirely. This is why the demand-token pool spans (seats + 1) suits - it spans exactly the decks on the table.

slotsBySeats is the authoritative layout table and is unchanged by the flat island - the island is the same SIZE, it just has no hierarchy. It follows seats+1 / seats / seats-1 by level, giving 6 / 9 / 12 tiles and therefore 12 / 18 / 24 delivery spaces.

demandTokensBySeats grew with the crate count: every tile now carries 2 crates, so the pool is tiles x 2 = 12 / 18 / 24, up from 10 / 16 / 22. The owner took a flat 4 tokens per suit at every seat count (one number to remember at the table) with the remainder in cornucopias, which puts the wild share at 0% / 11% / 17%. The 4-seat 17% is the highest the game has run and is the number to watch if the colour puzzle goes soft.

The pyramid layout is cosmetic in the strong sense now: no tile is adjacent to any other, adjacency is null by decision rather than by omission, and since the level gate was deleted nothing constrains WHICH tile you deliver to. Any tile with a free receipt space is legal on any turn.

Bookend rule: the art paints each row's first printed face (A1 / B1 / C1) as the island's left edge and its last (A5 / B4 / C3) as the right edge, so a row with n tiles in play uses the first (n - 1) printed faces plus the row-end face. The 3-tile level-1 row is therefore A1, A2, A5.
At 2 seats the lone level-3 tile is D1 rather than C1. D1 prints no mechanical difference from C1; it is a distinct illustration for the two-player board.
unresolved: D1 and C1 print identical cost and delivery capacity, and now that every tile is identical the two-seat substitution is purely illustrative. Confirm that is what is wanted, or drop D1 and let 2p use C3.
The flat 6-delivery end trigger is not scaled by seat count. If the 2-player game runs long at the table, the dial is either the trigger (a per-seat row) or slotsBySeats, not the VP.
